summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — removal, reasonable-efforts, and permanency requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of placement decisions

key_cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a Minnesota father's § 1983 claims, holding that a CHIPS petition filed two days after removal followed by a hearing within ten days supplied all the procedural process he was due.
key_cases.relevance: It states when a foster placement following removal satisfies due process because a prompt post-deprivation hearing followed.
key_cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity to state caseworkers, holding it was clearly established that children placed in state foster custody have a substantive due process right to protection, medical care and supervision.
key_cases.relevance: It establishes that once the state places a child in foster care it assumes an affirmative constitutional duty of protection and supervision.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we affirm the district court's denial of the Defendants' motion to dismiss based upon qualified immunity.

key_cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of L.K.
key_cases.holding: The court held that former foster parents were properly denied permissive intervention and that their third-party custody petition was properly dismissed, so they are not parties to the children's CHIPS case, and it vacated the court of appeals' constitutional ruling.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling Minnesota Supreme Court decision on whether former foster parents can contest a change in a child's foster placement.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the district court did not err in denying appellants' petition for permissive intervention and in dismissing their third-party custody petition.

state_agency.name: Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families
state_agency.hotline: No statewide hotline. Call the county or Tribal child protection agency where the child lives — the directory link is on dcyf.mn.gov/individuals-and-families/report-abuse

common_failures: Failure to consider less restrictive alternatives

timeline_requirements.deadline: 72 hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child taken into custody under Minn. Stat. § 260C.175, subd. 1, clause (1) or (2), item (ii)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; under Minn. Stat. § 260C.178, subd. 1(b) the child must be released to a parent, guardian, custodian, or other suitable person unless the court makes the endangerment findings in subd. 1(c).

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child placed in foster care by court order or voluntary placement agreement
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Minn. Stat. § 260C.212, subd. 1(a) sets the 30-day deadline for preparing the out-of-home placement plan.
